title: What are the challenges of microservices vs a monolithic application?
shortTitle: Challenges of microservices versus a monolithic application

s1_definition.profdef: A monolith is a single deployable unit where all modules share one process, one codebase, and one database, so calls are in-process method calls and transactions are local ACID transactions. Microservices split that unit into many independently deployable services, each owning its own database and communicating over the network. The split trades the simplicity of local calls and local transactions for independent scaling and deployment, and in return introduces distributed-system challenges: network latency and partial failure, eventual consistency instead of ACID, distributed tracing instead of a single stack trace, data duplication across service databases, and operational complexity from running many services.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India as one giant building where every clerk sits in the same hall. If Rajesh wants a transfer, one clerk walks three steps to the ledger desk and the cashier desk — fast, simple, and if the building is open everything works. That is a monolith. Now imagine the bank splits into separate buildings across the city: an Account building, a Payment building, a Notification building. Rajesh's transfer now needs a courier to carry forms between buildings. Couriers get stuck in traffic (network latency), sometimes a building is closed (partial failure), and you cannot lock all ledgers at once (no single transaction). You gained the ability to rebuild the Payment building without shutting the Account building, but you now have to manage a whole city.
s1_definition.oneliner: Monolith is simple but scales as one block; microservices scale and deploy independently but pay with network failure, eventual consistency, and operational complexity.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A monolith is a single deployable unit where all modules share one process, one codebase, and one database, so calls are in-process method calls and transactions are local ACID transactions. Microservices split that unit into many independently deployable services, each owning its own database and communicating over the network. The split trades the simplicity of local calls and local transactions for independent scaling and deployment, and in return introduces distributed-system challenges: network latency and partial failure, eventual consistency instead of ACID, distributed tracing instead of a single stack trace, data duplication across service databases, and operational complexity from running many services.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India as one giant building where every clerk sits in the same hall. If Rajesh wants a transfer, one clerk walks three steps to the ledger desk and the cashier desk — fast, simple, and if the building is open everything works. That is a monolith. Now imagine the bank splits into separate buildings across the city: an Account building, a Payment building, a Notification building. Rajesh's transfer now needs a courier to carry forms between buildings. Couriers get stuck in traffic (network latency), sometimes a building is closed (partial failure), and you cannot lock all ledgers at once (no single transaction). You gained the ability to rebuild the Payment building without shutting the Account building, but you now have to manage a whole city.

**One line to remember:** Monolith is simple but scales as one block; microservices scale and deploy independently but pay with network failure, eventual consistency, and operational complexity.

sections.s2_technical:
The first challenge is distributed transactions. In a monolith a transfer is one `@Transactional` method: debit and credit commit or roll back together. Across services you cannot span a database transaction over the network, so you adopt the Saga pattern with compensating actions. For example the payment saga debits the sender, then asks the Account Service to credit the receiver, and if that fails it compensates with a re-credit: `accountClient.credit(fromAccount, amount)`. You trade strong consistency for eventual consistency and must design every step to be undoable.

The second challenge is partial failure and latency. A local method call never "half works", but a network call can time out, be refused, or hang. You must wrap every remote call with a timeout, a retry, and a circuit breaker, for example `@CircuitBreaker(name="accountService", fallbackMethod="debitFallback")` so that when the Account Service is down the Payment Service fails fast instead of piling up threads. You also add bulkheads so one slow dependency cannot exhaust the whole thread pool.

The third challenge is data management. Database-per-service means the Payment Service cannot join against the Account Service's tables; it either calls the service or keeps a local read-model copy kept fresh by events, for example consuming `account-events` from Kafka. This causes data duplication and the need to reconcile. The fourth challenge is observability: a single request now crosses the gateway, payment, account, and notification services, so a plain stack trace is useless. You propagate a single traceId with Micrometer and view the waterfall in Zipkin. The fifth challenge is operational: many services mean many pipelines, service discovery, config servers, versioned contracts, and container orchestration. The senior-level nuance is that microservices are justified only when teams need independent deployment and scaling; otherwise you get a distributed monolith with all the pain and none of the benefit.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, Rajesh (SAV2001) transfers 50,000 rupees to Priya (CUR3001). Problem 1 — in the old monolith this was one database transaction, but after the split the balance lives in the Account Service and the transfer record lives in the Payment Service, so there is no single transaction to roll back. This is exactly the distributed-transaction challenge, and we solve it with a saga that debits, then credits, then compensates on failure. Problem 2 — the Account Service sometimes goes down for a deploy, and the naive Payment Service keeps calling it until all its threads are stuck waiting, taking the whole Payment Service down with it. This is exactly the partial-failure challenge, solved with a circuit breaker and timeout. Problem 3 — support staff cannot see why Rajesh's transfer is slow because the request touches three services and there is no single log. This is exactly the observability challenge, solved with a shared traceId.

The mini-project builds a small `TransferService` that plays the saga across an `AccountClient`, demonstrates the compensating re-credit when the credit step fails, and shows the circuit-breaker fallback when the Account Service is unavailable. Classes: `TransferService` (the saga orchestrator), `AccountClient` (remote calls with circuit breaker), `Account` (the familiar account with debit/credit), and a runnable `MonolithVsMicroservicesDemo` main that first shows the easy monolith path and then the harder distributed path.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer request of 50,000 rupees from Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001).

Step 1: The request enters `TransferService.transfer`. In the monolith this would be one transaction. Here, the service starts a saga and the money is still fully in Rajesh's account.

Step 2: The service calls `accountClient.debit("SAV2001", 50000)`. This is a remote call. On success Rajesh's balance drops to 950,000. The transfer record exists only in the Payment Service's own database — the Account Service never sees it.

Step 3: The service calls `accountClient.credit("CUR3001", 50000)`. On success Priya's balance rises to 300,000 and the saga completes with status COMPLETED.

Step 4: Now simulate the Account Service being down. The debit call throws because the network is unavailable. The saga has nothing to compensate yet, so it returns FAILED and no balance changed — Rajesh still has 1,000,000.

Step 5: If instead the debit had succeeded but the credit failed, the saga runs the compensating re-credit so Rajesh gets his 50,000 back, and the result is COMPENSATED. Eventual consistency is restored even though there was never a single transaction.

```text
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:01 INFO === Healthy path (both services up) ===
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:01 INFO REMOTE debit 50000 from SAV2001
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:01 INFO REMOTE credit 50000 to CUR3001
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:01 INFO Transfer SUCCESS SAV2001 to CUR3001 amount 50000
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:01 INFO Rajesh=950000 Priya=300000
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:01 INFO === Partial failure (Account Service down) ===
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:01 SEVERE Debit failed, nothing to compensate
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:01 INFO Result when service down: FAILED
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Transfer Request: Rs.50000 SAV2001 → CUR3001
    │
    ▼
  TransferService.transfer()  (SAGA orchestrator — NO single DB transaction)
    │
    ├─ SUCCESS PATH                      ├─ FAILURE PATH (Account Service down)
    │  debit(SAV2001) [remote]         │  debit(SAV2001) network error
    │  credit(CUR3001) [remote]        │  circuit breaker OPENS
    │  status: COMPLETED                 │  fail fast, no compensation needed
    ▼                                    ▼
  SAV2001: 1,000,000 → 950,000          SAV2001: 1,000,000 (unchanged)
  CUR3001: 250,000 → 300,000            CUR3001: 250,000 (unchanged)

    ├─ COMPENSATION PATH (debit ok, credit fails)
    │  debit(SAV2001)
    │  credit(CUR3001)
    │  credit(SAV2001)  ← compensating re-credit
    │  status: COMPENSATED
    ▼
  SAV2001 back to 1,000,000 (eventual consistency restored)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A monolith is a single deployable unit where all modules share one process and one database, so a transfer is just one local transaction and a single stack trace tells you everything. It is simple to build, test, and debug, and it is the right choice for a small team or an early-stage product. The problem is that it scales only as one block, every change redeploys the whole thing, and one memory leak can take down the entire application.

Microservices split that unit into independently deployable services, each owning its own database and talking over the network. In my banking work at National Bank of India, when Rajesh transfers money to Priya the balance lives in the Account Service and the transfer record lives in the Payment Service. The biggest challenge this creates is that there is no distributed transaction across services, so I use the Saga pattern: the Payment Service debits the sender, then credits the receiver, and if the credit fails it compensates by re-crediting the sender. We accept eventual consistency instead of strict ACID.

The second challenge is partial failure. A local method call never half-works, but a network call can time out or hang, so I wrap every remote call with a timeout, a retry, and a circuit breaker using Resilience4j. When the Account Service goes down for a deploy, the circuit breaker opens and the Payment Service fails fast instead of piling up threads and collapsing.

The third challenge is observability and operations. One request now crosses three services, so I propagate a single traceId with Micrometer and view the full waterfall in Zipkin, and I run many pipelines, a config server, service discovery, and container orchestration. The honest senior-level point I always make is that microservices are only worth this cost when teams genuinely need independent deployment and scaling; if they do not, you end up with a distributed monolith that has all the operational pain and none of the benefit.
